speaker: Petter Hörnfeldt
title: Ep16 - Interview with Petter Hoernfeldt - Mentour Pilot
question: In aviation media, what separates technical educators who build lasting audience trust from channels that struggle to retain viewers?
guest: You cannot start a channel with the explicit goal of growth or making money. The only way is being passionate about something and willing to share what you know—going in with the goal of giving to the audience so they leave feeling smarter. If you go in wanting growth and money, you want stuff from your audience, and people detect that immediately; if a message isn't genuine, they won't watch. When I started, if you looked online to see what being a pilot was like, you ended up in forums where pilots only went to vent their frustrations. Happy pilots didn't go online to talk—they went kitesurfing or spent time with family—so the internet gave a very skewed picture of aviation. I decided to be a positive, constructive outlet, talking about both positive and negative things constructively, the way we teach in the simulator. Then I found the vehicle to explain technical concepts through incidents and accidents, which had a general draw. I could use those accidents to explain how a hydraulic system works or what a flight management computer actually does—essentially tricking people into learning the theoretical part of a bigger story.

points.core: Audiences quickly detect extractive growth motives when creators prioritize money over value.
points.note: Accept: viewers sense insincerity when a channel optimizes for clicks, monetization, or growth rather than genuinely teaching and leaving the audience smarter. Do not credit: generic advice to 'be authentic' or 'make good content'.

points.core: Online pilot forums skew negative because satisfied pilots rarely vent online.
points.note: Accept: selection bias in aviation communities—content pilots spend free time offline while frustrated ones dominate forums, distorting public perception and leaving an opening for balanced voices. Do not credit: vague remarks that the internet is negative or toxic.

points.core: Constructive simulator-style critique builds credibility even when discussing negative aviation topics.
points.note: Accept: addressing failures, errors, or industry flaws in an objective, non-sensational, learning-focused tone rather than venting or sugarcoating. Do not credit: generic advice to stay positive or avoid controversy.

points.core: Real aviation accidents serve as narrative hooks for teaching dry technical systems.
points.note: Accept: embedding complex aircraft theory (like hydraulics or flight management computers) inside compelling real-world incident stories so general audiences stay engaged through technical explanations. Do not credit: generic advice to use storytelling or visual effects.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The dividing line is mostly credibility paired with restraint. Educators who earn lasting trust tend to have verifiable expertise (working pilots, engineers, controllers, or investigators) and stay visibly within it, saying "we don't know yet" after an accident instead of speculating for clicks. Channels like Mentour Pilot, blancolirio, and Air Safety Institute built their followings by waiting for preliminary reports, citing primary sources such as NTSB dockets and manufacturer documentation, and correcting themselves publicly when wrong.

They also explain the reasoning, not just the outcome: why a system is designed the way it is, what the crew likely saw, and how human factors shaped decisions. That treats viewers as capable of understanding complexity, and it avoids blaming individuals in ways that later prove unfair.

Channels that struggle usually show the opposite pattern: sensational thumbnails and titles the content doesn't deliver on, rapid speculation that ages badly, recycled footage with thin narration, and inconsistent quality or cadence. Aviation audiences include many professionals who spot errors quickly, so accuracy lapses are punished faster than in most niches.

This is my assessment from general observation, not from measured retention data.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In aviation media, lasting trust hinges on restraint, evidentiary discipline, and fidelity to aviation’s "just culture." Educators who retain audiences—especially after high-profile accidents—refuse to speculate beyond verified data such as ADS-B tracks, ATC recordings, weather reports, and official findings from investigative bodies like the NTSB. Rather than chasing algorithmic urgency with alarmist thumbnails or premature blame, they clearly distinguish confirmed facts from working hypotheses and openly revise their assessments as new evidence emerges.

Equally important is systemic framing. Trusted creators examine events through human factors, crew resource management, standard operating procedures, and aircraft systems design instead of villainizing individual pilots. They translate complex aerodynamics, avionics, and regulatory frameworks into accessible narratives without sacrificing technical accuracy, earning credibility with both curious laypeople and professional aviators—an audience notoriously quick to spot bluffing. Channels that struggle to retain viewers typically trade this rigor for drama, offering confident, oversimplified conclusions before flight recorders are even analyzed. When official reports eventually contradict those early hot takes, sensationalist channels lose authority, whereas disciplined educators compound trust over years.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Aviation educators who keep their audience's trust tend to share a few habits. They have real, checkable expertise, like Mentour Pilot's airline captain background, 74 Gear's working pilots, or the AOPA Air Safety Institute's instructors. They stay humble about what they don't know. After an accident, the trusted channels say "we don't know yet," wait for preliminary reports, point to NTSB or BEA findings, and avoid blaming dead crews before the evidence is in. Viewers notice when a speculative video turns out to be wrong. When these creators make a mistake, they correct it publicly. They explain the reasons behind procedures and systems, not just what happened, so viewers come away understanding more. Many also invite outside experts and use real data such as ADS-B tracks, ATC audio and checklists.

Channels that lose viewers usually do the opposite. They chase clicks with alarming thumbnails, rush out crash videos within hours, sensationalize tragedies, show credentials they can't back up, and pick up their facts from other channels. These habits can bring short bursts of views, but pilots and serious enthusiasts are a demanding audience and they eventually leave.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Trusted aviation educators show how they know what they know. They draw on flight manuals, investigation reports, and firsthand experience, make clear where the evidence ends, and correct mistakes openly. They also make technical ideas easy to follow. A cockpit walkthrough or a simple diagram can show why a crew made a decision and what options they had at the time.

Channels struggle to retain viewers when the title promises an explanation and the video delivers a recap, when jargon obscures the point, or when speculation gets airtime before the facts are established. A dramatic incident can earn a click. Viewers come back when each episode answers the question it raised and leaves them better equipped to understand the next flight, system, or incident.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Technical educators earn lasting trust when viewers can follow their reasoning. They might use a flight-deck diagram to explain what a crew could see at a critical moment, cite the investigation report, and say where the evidence leaves room for doubt. When new evidence changes the picture, they explain what changed and correct the earlier account.

Channels struggle to retain viewers when the experience repeatedly falls short of the promise. A dramatic title may earn a click, but a long preamble, unexplained jargon, or a confident claim about pilot error before the facts are in gives viewers less reason to return. The educators people come back to make each video worth their time and leave them better equipped to understand the next aviation story.
